pr_title: Fix start date for following sensor reschedule
pr_body:

Fixes #15645 that was likely the result of PR #9087.

The original optimization was well intentioned. However, because of the [task lifecycle](https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/2.2.2/concepts/tasks.html#task-instances), the task state is never in `UP_FOR_RESCHEDULE` when task is executed at the next poke interval. 

The scheduler updates the state for schedule-able tasks, which includes tasks with state `UP_FOR_RESCHEDULE`, to `SCHEDULED`. (see [source](https://github.com/apache/airflow/blob/9ac742885ffb83c15f7e3dc910b0cf9df073407a/airflow/models/dagrun.py#L884-L905)). This means that the original condition is never satisfied.

Instead of checking task state, we can check if mode is reschedule with the reschedule attribute if present.

issue_context.title: Sensor start_date gets updated for the same try in reschedule mode
issue_context.body:
**Apache Airflow version**: 2.0.0

**What happened**:

Sensor start_date gets updated to each time the task instance is rescheduled for the same try.

**What you expected to happen**:

I expect the `start_date` of a sensor task instance to remain the same within a given try. The `start_date` should be the start of first poke instead of the start time of the following rescheduled attempts. 

This behaviour does not match the description in the [source code](https://github.com/apache/airflow/blob/2.0.0/airflow/models/taskinstance.py#L982-L983).

>             # Set the task start date. In case it was re-scheduled use the initial
>             # start date that is recorded in task_reschedule table

Airflow did behave as expected in 1.10.x but it stopped in 2.0+.

**How to reproduce it**:

Run any sensors and watch the start_date value change at after each retry.

```python
with DAG(
        dag_id="check_dag",
        start_date=datetime(2021, 1, 1),
        schedule_interval='@daily',
        catchup=False,
) as dag:
    p = ExternalTaskSensor(
        task_id='sensor_task',
        external_dag_id='my_dag',
        mode='reschedule'
    )
```

review_comments: The  `reschedule` property is part of `BaseSensorOperator` , but this is not the only kind of reschedulable operator.   Any operator can raise `AirflowRescheduleException` to  reschedule and may not have the `reschedule` property.  So I don't think we use this property  to infer what to do here.

Ahh, good point!

Since any operator can raise `AirflowRescheduleException`, how would I distinguish between tasks that are being rescheduled? Would I need to query the `task_reschedule` table for all tasks? This would remove the original optimization though maybe it doesn't make sense to have it in the first place.

> Since any operator can raise AirflowRescheduleException, how would I distinguish between tasks that are being rescheduled? Would I need to query the task_reschedule table for all tasks? This would remove the original optimization though maybe it doesn't make sense to have it in the first place.


with the caveat that i don't know this code all that well...

so, what you have pointed out is that `check_and_change_state_before_execution` never runs until after state is already flipped to `scheduled` by `schedule_tis`, right?  that makes sense.

i'm not seeing anything that's already there that would allow us to determine whether the TI is resuming from a reschedule or some other case.  i think any solution (apart from just reverting the optimization and looking up the reschedules) is likely to be rather involved.

e.g. one option would be to split up the task states.  we could think of some of the states as being different "kinds" of state. some states overlap e.g. you could say a task is "up for retry" from the moment a task fails until the moment it is actually running again.  meanwhile the task can cycle through many other "states" in this period of time.

Along these lines, we could think of these as one kind of state (call it "execution state"):

```
none
scheduled
queued
running
shutdown
restarting
paused  <-- just made this up
done <-- made this up too
```

To this we might add a category called "resolutions"

```
success
failed
skipped
upstream_failed
removed
```

Tasks in a `done` state would have _one_ of the above resolutions.

Then finally we could have one more attribute, named _what_ i'm not sure -- but it could have these values:
```
up_for_retry
up_for_reschedule
deferred
```

These are the _reasons_ why a task is not actively running but also not done.

By splitting things up in this way you would know, when you are flipping a task from queued to running for example, whether it's a resuming after a retry, or a reschedule, or a deferral.

But, I doubt there would be appetite to do something like this.

Maybe @ashb or @kaxil would have other ideas?
